title: 1971 AHSME Problem 29
statement: Given the progression \[ \begin{gathered} 10^{\frac{1}{11}},10^{\frac{2}{11}},10^{\frac{3}{11}},\\ 10^{\frac{4}{11}},\ldots,10^{\frac{n}{11}}, \end{gathered} \] the least positive integer \(n\) such that the product of the first \(n\) terms exceeds \(100{,}000\) is:

solutions.text:
The product is \[ 10^{\frac{1+2+\cdots+n}{11}}=10^{\frac{n(n+1)}{22}}. \] It exceeds \(100{,}000=10^5\) exactly when \(n(n+1)\gt110.\) For \(n=10\) there is equality, while \(n=11\) works.

Therefore, the correct answer is E.
hints: Add the exponents when multiplying the terms
Require \(\frac{n(n+1)}{22}\gt5\), noting that equality is not enough
